content: The definition, agreement, and practical application of units of measurement have been fundamental to human progress from ancient times to the present day. Historically, disparate systems of measurement were widespread, but today, the International System of Units (SI), the modern form of the metric system, serves as the global standard. The SI system has been adopted or is in the process of being adopted worldwide. The United States is one of the last countries to fully adopt the system, but its use is steadily increasing even there. In trade, weights and measures are often regulated by governments to ensure fairness and transparency. The Bureau International des Poids et Mesures (BIPM) is responsible for maintaining worldwide uniformity of measurements and ensuring their traceability to the SI system. Metrology, the science of measurement, focuses on developing nationally and internationally accepted units of weights and measures. In physics and metrology, units serve as standards for measuring physical quantities, requiring precise definitions to ensure their utility. The reproducibility of experimental results, a cornerstone of the scientific method, is facilitated by a standardized system of units. Scientific systems of units are refinements of the weights and measures originally developed for commercial purposes. Fields such as science, medicine, and engineering often require units of measurement that are larger or smaller than those used in everyday life and demand greater precision in their application. The careful selection of measurement units can assist researchers in solving complex problems, as seen in techniques like dimensional analysis. A unit of measurement is a standardized quantity of a physical property used to express other quantities of the same property. Units of measurement were among the earliest tools invented by humans. Primitive societies required basic measures for tasks such as constructing dwellings, making clothing, or bartering food and raw materials. The earliest known uniform systems of weights and measures emerged in the 4th and 3rd millennia BCE among the ancient civilizations of Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, and possibly Elam in Persia. Many early systems were based on parts of the human body and natural surroundings as measuring instruments. Our current understanding of early weights and measures is derived from a variety of historical sources. Before the global adoption of the metric system, numerous systems of measurement were in use, often based on the dimensions of the human body. These systems varied not only by location but also from person to person. Since the adoption of the original metric system in France in 1791, several metric systems of units have evolved. The current international standard is the International System of Units (SI). A key feature of modern systems is standardization, where each unit has a universally recognized size. Both the Imperial units and US customary units are derived from earlier English units. Imperial units were primarily used in the British Commonwealth and the former British Empire, while US customary units remain the primary system in the United States, despite Congress legally authorizing metric measures in 1866. Some steps toward metrication have been made in the US, such as redefining basic units to align with SI units. The above systems of units are based on arbitrary unit values formalized as standards. However, some unit values occur naturally in science, and systems based on these are called natural units. Similarly, atomic units (au) are a convenient system of measurement used in atomic physics. Additionally, a variety of unconventional and non-standard units may be encountered, such as the ton of TNT, the Hiroshima atomic bomb, or the weight of an elephant. Different systems of units are based on varying choices of fundamental units. The most widely used system is the International System of Units (SI), which includes seven base units. All other SI units are derived from these base units. For most physical quantities, a unit is essential to communicate their values. For example, describing a specific length without a unit is impossible, as a reference is required to make sense of the value. However, not all quantities require unique units. Using physical laws, units of some quantities can be expressed as combinations of units of other quantities, reducing the need for a large set of units. These fundamental units are referred to as base units, while others are derived units. Derived units are a matter of convenience, as they can be expressed in terms of base units. The choice of base units is arbitrary. The SI base units are not the smallest possible set; smaller sets have been defined, including systems where electric and magnetic fields share the same unit. Such systems are based on physical laws demonstrating that electric and magnetic fields are different manifestations of the same phenomenon. In some scientific fields, these alternative systems are preferred over the SI system. Any value of a physical quantity is expressed as a comparison to a unit of that quantity. For example, the value of a physical quantity ( Q ) is written as the product of a unit and a numerical factor. In formulas, the unit can be treated as a type of physical dimension, as seen in dimensional analysis. A distinction must be made between units and standards. A unit is fixed by its definition and is independent of physical conditions such as temperature. In contrast, a standard is a physical realization of a unit and is valid only under specific physical conditions. For instance, the metre is a unit, while a metal bar is a standard. One metre remains the same length regardless of temperature, but a metal bar will measure one metre only at a specific temperature. When performing calculations with units, treat them like variables. Only add like terms. Dividing a unit by itself yields a unitless one. Multiplying two different units results in a new unit, such as metres per second (m/s) for speed in the SI system. Some units have special names but should be treated as their equivalents. For example, one newton (N) is equivalent to one kilogram-metre per second squared (kg·m/s²). This allows for multiple designations of units, such as surface tension being expressed as either newtons per metre (N/m) or kilograms per second squared (kg/s²). Converting a physical value from one unit to another involves comparing different standard physical values. For example, to convert a value in feet per second to miles per hour, find the relationships between the units (1 mile = 5280 feet, 1 hour = 3600 seconds), construct a fraction with a value of one that cancels the original units, and multiply the original value by this conversion factor. Since conversion factors have a numerical value of one, multiplying by them does not change the physical value. The importance of agreed units is exemplified by the failure of the NASA Mars Climate Orbiter in September 1999. The spacecraft was destroyed due to a miscommunication about force values, as different computer programs used different units of measurement (newton versus pound-force). This error resulted in the loss of significant effort, time, and money. Similarly, on April 15, 1999, Korean Air cargo flight 6316 crashed due to confusion between tower instructions (in metres) and altimeter readings (in feet), resulting in the deaths of three crew members and five people on the ground, as well as injuries to 37 others.
